subject: english-literature
title: Setting, Technology and Gothic Geography
welcome_lead: Map the novel's movement between Transylvania and London and analyse how Stoker fuses ancient Gothic setting with late-Victorian technology.
meta_desc: A-Level Edexcel adventure on setting, technology, and Gothic geography in Stoker's Dracula.
final_note: Stoker's Gothic is uniquely modern: the Count crosses Europe by sailing-ship, but is tracked by phonograph, typewriter and telegraph.

concepts.def: The Borgo Pass castle, dilapidated and labyrinthine; Gothic prototype of confinement and aristocratic decay.
The schooner that carries Dracula from Varna to Whitby; the captain's log is one of the novel's most powerful set-pieces.
The Yorkshire seaside town where Dracula makes landfall; Stoker visited in 1890 and based Dracula's arrival on local folklore.
The decayed London estate Dracula purchases as his base; a Gothic ruin embedded in the modern metropolis.
Typewriters, phonographs, shorthand, telegrams, Kodak cameras, blood transfusion — modernity's tools weaponised against the ancient.
Christopher Craft's name for the male hunters (Harker, Seward, Holmwood, Morris, Van Helsing) who pursue Dracula.

walkthroughs.body_html: The novel moves from Castle Dracula's labyrinth via the Borgo Pass, through the Carpathians, by ship from Varna to Whitby, then to London — Piccadilly, Hampstead, Purfleet's Carfax estate, finally returning across Europe to the Borgo Pass for the climax. The geography is itself an argument: Gothic horror originates in the imperial periphery, threatens the metropolis, and must be expelled. Critics including Franco Moretti map this trajectory onto economic anxiety about peripheral capital.

walkthroughs.h2: The Demeter at Tate Hill Pier
walkthroughs.body_html: The Russian schooner Demeter arrives at Whitby during a storm with all hands lost; a great dog leaps ashore. Stoker drew on the real 1885 wreck of the Dmitry at Whitby, transcribing details from local papers. Mina records the event from St Mary's churchyard. The Whitby chapters demonstrate Stoker's documentary realism: precise tide times, local dialect, real topography — a Gothic anchored in geographic specificity.

Friedrich Kittler in Discourse Networks 1900 argues that Dracula is defeated by the very technologies that define 1890s information culture: Mina's typewriter collates handwritten journals; Seward's phonograph captures spoken testimony; telegrams coordinate transcontinental pursuit. The Count, an oral, feudal entity who fears mirrors, is overwhelmed by mechanical reproduction. Stoker dramatises modernity's epistemic confidence.
